A bier is a flat, portable frame or platform used to carry a coffin — or sometimes a dead body — from one place to another, usually during a funeral.

Think of it as a kind of stretcher designed specifically for the dead. Just as hospital workers carry an injured person on a stretcher, mourners carry the deceased on a bier.

A traditional bier is a rectangular wooden frame with two long poles running along its sides. These poles stick out at both ends, giving pallbearers (the people who carry the coffin at a funeral) a place to grip and lift. The coffin is laid on top of the flat surface.

Some biers have legs and function more like a stand or table, designed to hold the coffin at a comfortable height — for example, in the middle of a church during a funeral service, so the congregation can see the coffin clearly.

Others are mounted on wheels, almost like a cart, making it easier to roll the coffin into or out of a church or hearse.

Here is a typical scene: A person dies. Their body is placed in a coffin. The coffin is then set on a bier. Pallbearers lift the bier by its handles and carry it — through a church, down a path, or to the graveside — as part of the funeral procession.

In older times, before motor vehicles became common, the bier was the main way coffins were moved through the streets of a town during a funeral. People would line the roads, hats in hand, as the bier passed by.
How It Differs from Similar Things

It is easy to confuse a bier with related objects. Here is how they are different:

  • The coffin is the box that holds the body. The bier is what carries the coffin. Think of it this way: the coffin holds the person, and the bier holds the coffin.
  • A hearse is the vehicle (a car or horse-drawn carriage) that transports the coffin to the burial site. The bier is non-motorized — it is carried by people, not driven.
  • A catafalque is a grand, heavily decorated platform used specifically for state funerals or the funerals of important public figures — kings, presidents, generals. It is essentially a very elaborate bier. When a head of state dies and their coffin is displayed in a great hall for the public to pay respects, the coffin rests on a catafalque.
  • A stretcher looks similar to a bier in shape, but it is used to carry living people (usually injured or ill). A bier is used exclusively for the dead.
Where You Will Encounter This Word

"Bier" is not a word you will hear in everyday casual conversation. It lives mostly in:

  • Literature and poetry, especially older works, where death and funerals are described with formal, solemn language. ("They laid him upon the bier and carried him to his rest.")
  • Religious and ceremonial contexts, where the precise vocabulary of funeral rites is important.
  • Historical writing, since the bier was a central part of burial customs for centuries before modern funeral vehicles took over.

In modern life, the actual object still exists — wooden frames used to carry coffins in churches and graveyards are still in use — but the average person rarely uses the word "bier" to describe it.

"Bier" sounds exactly like "beer" (the drink) when spoken aloud in English. They are completely unrelated words that just happen to sound the same. This kind of word pair is called a homophone. If you encounter "bier" in a text, the surrounding context — a funeral, death, mourning — will always make it clear which word is meant.

A bier is the frame or platform that carries a coffin during a funeral, serving as a kind of stretcher for the dead — once shouldered by pallbearers through the streets, now more often seen inside churches or moved on wheels.
